questions.q: Recall the two discussion prompts given in the NCERT textbook under "Talking About the Text" for "The Luncheon."
questions.a: The two prompts are: (1) "People with foibles are often not conscious of them" and (2) "The author's attempts at keeping up his pretence of friendliness while he was mentally preoccupied with the expense of the luncheon." A wrong answer (e.g., listing comprehension questions from "Understanding the Text") reveals the student cannot distinguish between written comprehension tasks and oral discussion prompts, indicating they haven't internalized the different cognitive demands of speaking vs. writing.

questions.q: Explain in your own words what "foible" means in the context of the first discussion prompt, and identify which character in "The Luncheon" it applies to.
questions.a: A foible is a minor weakness or eccentricity in character; in the story, it applies to the lady who claims "I never eat more than one thing" while ordering multiple expensive dishes, revealing her lack of self-awareness about her gluttony and manipulativeness. A wrong answer that defines foible as "a lie" or "a major flaw" or applies it to the narrator shows the student confuses the lady's unconscious self-deception with deliberate deceit, missing the nuance that foibles are unconscious — the lady genuinely believes her own performance.

questions.q: During a group discussion on Prompt 2, a peer says: "The narrator is hypocritical because he judges the lady but flatters her to get a free meal." Using textual evidence, formulate a spoken response that acknowledges the peer's point but reframes it using the concept of dramatic irony.
questions.a: Response: "I see why you'd call it hypocrisy, but the text frames it as dramatic irony — we know he has only 80 francs (page 99) and is 'too young to have learned to say no to a woman,' so his friendliness is survival, not flattery. The humour comes from the gap between his internal panic ('my heart sank,' 'panic seized me') and his polite exterior ('hospitable still, but not exactly effusive')." A wrong response that simply agrees or disagrees without textual anchoring shows the student treats discussion as opinion-sharing rather than evidence-based literary analysis.

questions.q: Compare how the first-person narrative serves the discussion of humour in "The Luncheon" versus how it would function in a third-person retelling. Provide one specific textual example.
questions.a: First-person gives direct access to the narrator's internal calculations ("I had eighty francs... a modest luncheon should not cost more than fifteen") and visceral reactions ("my heart sank," "panic seized me"), creating situational irony — we suffer his anxiety while watching the lady's oblivious consumption. In third-person, the humour would shift to external observation, losing the intimate comic tension. Example: the narrator's thought "I would put my hand in my pocket and with a dramatic cry start up and say it had been picked" is funny because we hear his desperate interior monologue; third-person would merely report "he considered pretending to be robbed," diluting the self-deprecating humour. A wrong answer that says "first-person is more emotional" without contrasting the specific mechanism of irony shows superficial understanding of narrative point of view.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "The story's ending — 'Today she weighs twenty-one stone' — validates the narrator's revenge and makes the story a triumph of justice." Defend or challenge using the concept of authorial tone.
questions.a: Challenge: The ending uses comedic exaggeration ("twenty-one stone" = 133 kg, physically improbable) and the narrator's own admission "I do not believe that I am a vindictive man, but when the immortal gods take a hand..." frames the outcome as divine comedy, not moral justice. The tone is self-mocking — he calls himself a "humorist" — suggesting the revenge is absurd, not righteous. A wrong answer that agrees with the claim misses Maugham's ironic distance: the narrator's "complacency" is itself a foible, mirroring the lady's lack of self-awareness. The story ends on a joke, not a judgment.

questions.q: Create a 60-second opening statement for a group discussion on: "Maugham uses food as a metaphor for power dynamics in 'The Luncheon'." Include a thesis, two textual anchors, and a linking question for peers.
questions.a: Sample opening: "My thesis: food operates as currency and control. First, the lady weaponizes the menu — she orders caviare, salmon, asparagus, peaches knowing the narrator pays, turning hospitality into extraction (page 100-102). Second, the narrator's mutton chop — 'the cheapest dish' — marks his powerlessness; his hunger becomes literal and metaphorical. The linking question: 'Does the narrator regain any power by the end, or does the "twenty-one stone" joke just invert the dynamic?' A poor answer would list food items without connecting to power, or omit the linking question, showing the student doesn't grasp discussion as a collaborative, inquiry-driven process."

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Speaking and Listening: Discussion Points is the oral ______ skill of articulating literary analysis, interpreting textual evidence, and engaging in structured academic dialogue about a text's themes, characters, and narrative techniques, using precise vocabulary and logical argumentation suitable for Class 11 CBSE assessment criteria.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you're in a literature circle where your group must discuss: "Is the lady in 'The Luncheon' deliberately ______ or genuinely oblivious?" You'll start by recalling the textual details — her repeated "I never eat more than one thing" while ordering caviare, salmon, asparagus, ice-cream, coffee, and peaches.
What is Speaking and Listening? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Speaking and Listening: Discussion Points is the oral communication skill of articulating literary analysis, interpreting textual evidence, and engaging in structured academic dialogue about a text's themes, characters, and narrative techniques, using precise vocabulary and logical argumentation suitable for Class 11 CBSE assessment.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: You'll practice phrasing your point as: "The text shows she orders five courses while claiming to eat 'one thing' (page ______), which suggests..." Finally, you'll learn to build on a peer's point: "Adding to Rohan's observation about her teeth description, the 'white and large and even' imagery reinforces her performative consumption." The key insight: effective literary discussion requires evidence-anchored claims, not opinions.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Speaking and Listening?
questions.a: Students treat "Speaking and Listening" as informal chat — sharing personal opinions ("I think the lady was rude") instead of textual analysis ("The text shows the lady orders asparagus after claiming she 'never eats anything for luncheon,' demonstrating performative modesty").

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must independently lead or contribute to a 3-minute structured discussion on "The Luncheon" by: (1) presenting a clear thesis about irony/humour/character with textual evidence, (2) responding to a peer's point by agreeing, extending, or challenging with a specific textual reference, and (3) synthesizing the discussion into a.
